question: Why is it recommended to separate CartStateContext and CartDispatchContext instead of using a single CartContext?

options.text: The code looks cleaner and more concise
options.explanation: This is subjective, and the pattern actually adds more code. The reason for separation is performance.

options.text: Components using only dispatch will not re-render when state changes
options.explanation: dispatch from useReducer is stable — React guarantees its reference does not change. If a component is subscribed only to CartDispatchContext, it will not re-render when items are added to the cart.

options.text: Two contexts allow different data types
options.explanation: TypeScript allows typing any context. Separation is not about typing.

options.text: Context cannot store state and functions simultaneously
options.explanation: Context can store any values, including objects with state and functions.

question: When should you use useReducer instead of useState?

options.text: When transition logic is complex and conditional
options.explanation: A reducer is a pure function that is easy to read, test, and extend. Complex logic in setState callbacks is unreadable.

options.text: When you need to log or replay action history
options.explanation: Actions explicitly describe what happened. This simplifies debugging and allows implementing undo/redo.

options.text: When multiple state fields always update together
options.explanation: For example, { loading, data, error } — they are always linked. useReducer updates them atomically in one dispatch.

options.text: When a component renders a list of 100+ elements
options.explanation: The number of rendered elements is not related to choosing useState vs useReducer. This is a render optimization issue, not state structure.

question: You have a NotificationProvider. How should you correctly clean up setTimeout timers when the component unmounts?

options.text: Store timers in useState and call clearTimeout in handlers
options.explanation: On unmount, handlers are not called — timers will leak. Also setState on an unmounted component will cause a warning.

options.text: Call clearTimeout in componentWillUnmount
options.explanation: componentWillUnmount is a class component method. Functional components use the cleanup function from useEffect.

options.text: React automatically clears all timers on unmount
options.explanation: React does not clear timers — this is the developer's responsibility. An uncleared timer will keep running and may call setState on an already unmounted component.

options.text: Return a cleanup function from useEffect: return () => { timers.forEach(clearTimeout) }
options.explanation: useEffect with an empty dependency array runs once on mount. The returned function is called on unmount. This is the standard cleanup pattern.

question: You are building a cart. The AddToCartButton component uses only dispatch({ type: 'ADD', item }). Is it true that it will NOT re-render when items are added to the cart?

options.text: Only if AddToCartButton is wrapped in React.memo
options.explanation: React.memo protects against re-renders from props, but not from context changes. Context separation solves this more reliably.

options.text: Yes, if the component is subscribed only to CartDispatchContext (not CartStateContext)
options.explanation: dispatch from useReducer is stable — React guarantees its reference does not change between renders. CartDispatchContext.Provider value does not change, so consumers do not re-render.

options.text: Yes, but only in React 18+ thanks to automatic batching
options.explanation: Batching merges multiple setState calls into one render, but does not prevent re-renders of components subscribed to a changed context.

options.text: No, any dispatch causes a re-render of the entire tree
options.explanation: Re-renders are triggered by context value changes. If CartDispatchContext.value (dispatch) did not change — consumers do not re-render.

question: Which of the following are advantages of the createStore pattern with selectors over direct useContext?

options.text: A component can subscribe to only the needed part of state
options.explanation: A selector describes which slice of state the component needs. Changes to unrelated state parts do not cause a re-render.

options.text: Eliminates the need to write boilerplate for each new Provider
options.explanation: The createStore factory creates a Provider + two contexts + two hooks in one call. A new store is added in one line.

options.text: All of the above options are incorrect
options.explanation: Some of the listed options are indeed correct.

options.text: Allows creating independent stores for different areas of the application
options.explanation: Each createStore call creates a new pair of contexts. Stores are fully independent.

options.text: Automatically persists state in localStorage
options.explanation: createStore does not work with localStorage by default. This must be implemented separately.

question: In which case is Context + useReducer NOT the optimal solution?

options.text: Application theme (light/dark) at the app-wide scale
options.explanation: Theme is an ideal case for Context. Simple state, needed globally, changes rarely.

options.text: Notification system with auto-dismiss
options.explanation: Notifications are perfectly implemented via Context + useReducer or useState. Limited scope, simple queue.

options.text: Server data cache with normalization, pagination, and invalidation
options.explanation: A data cache with this level of complexity is better handled by specialized tools: React Query, SWR, or Redux Toolkit Query. Context is not suitable for complex caching.

options.text: Shopping cart: add, remove, clear
options.explanation: Cart is a classic example for Context + useReducer. Limited scope, clear actions, moderate complexity.

question: You have a NotificationProvider. You want the notify function to be stable (not recreated on every render). How should it be correctly defined?

options.text: const notify = useCallback((message) => { setNotifications(prev => [...prev, ...]) }, [])
options.explanation: useCallback with an empty dependency array creates the function once. Updating state via an updater function (prev => ...) does not require adding state to dependencies.

options.text: const notifyRef = useRef((message) => { setNotifications(prev => [...prev, ...]) })
options.explanation: useRef is stable, but the function in ref is not updated when closures change. This leads to stale closure problems.

options.text: const notify = useMemo(() => (message) => { ... }, [])
options.explanation: Technically works, but semantically incorrect. useMemo is for values, useCallback is for functions. Use the right tool.

options.text: const notify = (message) => { setNotifications(prev => [...prev, ...]) }
options.explanation: Without useCallback the function is recreated on every Provider render. All NotificationContext consumers will get a new reference and re-render.

question: A reducer receives action { type: 'DECREMENT', id: 'p1' } for an item with quantity: 1. How should this case be handled correctly?

options.text: Throw an error: throw new Error('Cannot decrement below 0')
options.explanation: Errors in a reducer will crash the component. A reducer must always return a valid state.

options.text: First check quantity and if === 1 — dispatch REMOVE instead of DECREMENT
options.explanation: Dispatching actions inside a reducer is not allowed — a reducer must be a pure synchronous function without side effects.

options.text: Set quantity to 0: items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, quantity: 0 } : i)
options.explanation: Quantity 0 makes no sense in a cart — an item with zero quantity takes up space and confuses the user.

options.text: Decrease quantity and filter out items with quantity <= 0
options.explanation: The correct approach: first decrease quantity, then filter. This is an atomic operation without an intermediate invalid state.

question: Which of the following statements are true for the reducer function in useReducer?

options.text: A reducer can perform async operations (fetch, setTimeout)
options.explanation: A reducer must be a synchronous pure function. For async operations use useEffect, Redux Thunk, or Redux Saga.

options.text: A reducer should return a new state object only when changes occur, otherwise return the same object
options.explanation: If nothing changed (default case), return the same state object. React compares by reference and will skip a re-render.

options.text: A reducer must not mutate the input state
options.explanation: React uses referential equality to detect changes. Mutating state will not trigger a re-render and leads to unpredictable behavior.

options.text: A reducer must be a pure function
options.explanation: A pure function: same input → same output, no side effects. React may call the reducer multiple times in StrictMode.

question: You use createStore with a selector `useStore(s => s.todos.filter(t => !t.done))`. On every dispatch (even unrelated to todos) the component re-renders. What is the problem?

options.text: The selector returns a new array every time, React considers the value changed
options.explanation: filter() creates a new array on every call. React compares the selector result via ===. A new array !== the old array, even if the contents are the same. Solution: use useMemo or a library with deepEqual comparison.

options.text: createStore does not support complex selectors with filter
options.explanation: createStore supports any selector function. The problem is not in createStore, but in the referential equality of the result.

options.text: You should return a string or number from the selector instead of an array
options.explanation: The return type does not solve the architectural issue. If you need an array — use memoization.

options.text: You should wrap the component in React.memo
options.explanation: React.memo protects against re-renders from props, but not from context changes. This will not fix the problem.
